title: Eulerian and Hamiltonian Graphs
quickIdea: Euler is a degree-parity question with a complete answer, while Hamilton has no usable criterion, so GATE asks only the sufficient conditions and the standard counterexamples.
remember: An Euler circuit uses every edge exactly once and returns to its start; it exists exactly when the graph is connected after isolated vertices are ignored and every degree is even.
An Euler path uses every edge exactly once without returning; it exists exactly when there are 0 or 2 vertices of odd degree, and the odd vertices are then its endpoints.
A connected graph is Eulerian exactly when its edge set splits into edge-disjoint cycles.
A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex exactly once; no simple necessary and sufficient condition is known, and deciding Hamiltonicity is NP-complete.
Dirac's condition: if n is at least 3 and every degree is at least n/2 then the graph is Hamiltonian. It is sufficient but not necessary, since C_5 is Hamiltonian with all degrees 2.
K_{m,n} has a Hamiltonian cycle exactly when m = n is at least 2, and K_n for odd n splits into (n-1)/2 edge-disjoint Hamiltonian cycles.
The Petersen graph has a Hamiltonian path and no Hamiltonian cycle, which is the standard example separating the two.

example.prompt: Does K_{2,3} have an Euler circuit, an Euler path, or neither?
example.work: The degrees are 3, 3 for the two vertices on the small side and 2, 2, 2 for the other side. Exactly two vertices have odd degree, and the graph is connected, so an Euler path exists; an Euler circuit needs all degrees even, which fails.
example.answer: An Euler path but no Euler circuit.

gateAngle: GATE asks Euler parity as a one-liner and uses K_{3,3} or the Petersen graph as the 'path but no cycle' example, which is exactly how GATE CSE 2022 Q.40 used Petersen.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Does K_{3,3} have an Euler path?
variations.answer: No. All six vertices have degree 3, so there are six odd-degree vertices, and an Euler path allows at most two.
variations.why: The parity test rules out both the circuit (all even) and the path (exactly two odd).

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Can a graph have a Hamiltonian path but no Hamiltonian cycle?
variations.answer: Yes. The Petersen graph has a Hamiltonian path and no Hamiltonian cycle.
variations.why: Deleting one edge of a Hamiltonian cycle leaves a Hamiltonian path, but the converse fails, and there is no parity-style test for cycles.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Into how many edge-disjoint Hamiltonian cycles does K_5 split?
variations.answer: 2, which is (5-1)/2; K_5 has 10 edges and each Hamiltonian cycle uses 5 of them.
variations.why: For odd n the complete graph K_n decomposes into (n-1)/2 edge-disjoint Hamiltonian cycles.

trap.what: Treating Dirac's degree condition as necessary, or assuming that an Euler path needs all degrees even.
trap.why: Dirac only guarantees a Hamiltonian cycle; C_5 is Hamiltonian and violates it. An Euler path needs at most two odd-degree vertices, because every time the walk passes through a vertex it uses two edges.
trap.counterexample: C_5 is Hamiltonian with delta = 2 and n/2 = 2.5, so Dirac's hypothesis fails; K_{2,3} has an Euler path and two odd-degree vertices.

check.question: K_4 with one pendant edge attached has how many odd-degree vertices, and does it have an Euler path?
check.answer: Four odd-degree vertices, so it has neither an Euler path nor an Euler circuit.
check.explanation: The four K_4 vertices have degree 3 each, and attaching the pendant edge raises the attachment vertex to degree 4 and gives the pendant vertex degree 1, leaving odd degrees 4, 3, 3, 3, 1. Four odd vertices exceed the two an Euler path allows.

sourceLine: Euler and Hamiltonian definitions, the parity criterion and the edge-disjoint Hamiltonian decomposition of K_n for odd n: GATE Overflow GO Classroom deck (English, read in part). Dirac and the Petersen counterexample from West. Standard references used to verify, never copied: Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, ch. 10; West, Introduction to Graph Theory (Brooks, Dirac, Koenig, chromatic polynomial); CLRS ch. 22 (articulation points, bridges) and ch. 26 (bipartite matching); Diestel, Graph Theory (Menger). Every parity claim and the K_5 decomposition are recomputed in scripts/validate.py.
